title: Nu Holdings Scales in Mexico: Can It Unlock New Revenue Streams?
detail:
Nu Holdings Scales in Mexico: Can It Unlock New Revenue Streams?
Rohit Vasant Fatarpekar
Tue, November 24, 2026 at 12:13 PM EST 3 min read
NU
ITUB
MELI
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Nu Holdings NU is expanding its presence in Mexico, supported by growing customer adoption, its transition to a full-fledged bank and favorable digital banking trends. In the third quarter of 2026, the company's Mexican customer base increased 27% year over year to 16.6 million, representing 17% of the country's adult population. With 870,000 customer additions during the quarter, NU strengthened its position as Mexico's largest digital bank.

The transition to a bank marks an important milestone. Deposit insurance coverage increased sixteenfold, from approximately $12,000 to $195,000 per customer. Banking status also enables the company to offer payroll accounts, providing opportunities to capture salary deposits, deepen customer relationships and generate additional revenues through cross-selling financial products.

Nu Holdings is also focusing on improving its funding economics in Mexico. At the third quarter-end, deposits stood at $5.3 billion. The company is shifting toward lower-cost deposits while maintaining ample liquidity. Greater payroll account adoption could build a more stable and cost-effective funding base, supporting lending growth, net interest income and profitability.

Mexico's push toward digital payments presents another growth opportunity. On Oct. 20, 2026, the country's Congress approved legislation promoting digital payments and reducing reliance on cash. Greater digital adoption could provide richer transaction data, improve credit underwriting and expand lending opportunities.

Management sees substantial growth potential in Mexico, where credit card penetration remains at around 12%. Under its base-case scenario, the Mexican business could reach 70% of the scale of its Brazilian operations, while greater digitalization could enable it to match Brazil's scale. Nu Holdings' banking transition, expanding lending opportunities and greater scope for cross-selling financial products could help the company unlock additional revenue streams in Mexico.

How Do Itaú Unibanco & MercadoLibre Compete?

Itaú Unibanco ITUB competes with Nu Holdings through its extensive banking network, digital financial services and diversified product offerings, including credit cards, personal loans and investments. Its established presence across Brazil, Chile, Paraguay and Uruguay strengthens its regional competitive positioning. As of Sept. 2026, ITUB has a presence in 18 countries and territories.

MercadoLibre MELI, through its fintech platform Mercado Pago, competes with Nu Holdings by offering digital payments, credit, savings and investment solutions across Latin America. Its established e-commerce ecosystem facilitates customer acquisition and cross-selling opportunities, particularly in Brazil, Mexico and Argentina. In the third quarter of 2026, Mercado Pago's monthly active users increased 29% year over year to 93 million.

title: MercadoLibre vs. Target: Which Stock Looks More Compelling Now?
detail:
MercadoLibre vs. Target: Which Stock Looks More Compelling Now?
Vrishali Bagree
Tue, November 24, 2026 at 8:32 AM EST 6 min read
MELI
TGT
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

MercadoLibre, Inc. MELI and Target Corporation TGT are pursuing strategic initiatives to strengthen customer engagement, expand revenue opportunities and build sustainable earnings power. Their latest quarterly results offer insights into the effectiveness of these investments and their potential to generate long-term shareholder value.

MercadoLibre is a leading e-commerce and financial technology company in Latin America, operating across online marketplaces, digital payments, lending, logistics and advertising. MELI is benefiting from the increasing adoption of online shopping and digital financial services. Target, a prominent U.S. general merchandise retailer, is strengthening its business through differentiated merchandise, competitive pricing, store modernization, digital innovation and an enhanced shopping experience.

MercadoLibre and Target have market capitalizations of approximately $72.2 billion and $76.1 billion, respectively.

The Case for MELI

MercadoLibre continues to capitalize on the structural shift toward online commerce and digital financial services across Latin America. Its third-quarter 2026 net revenues and financial income increased 45% year over year, with market share gains across Brazil, Mexico and Argentina. Expanded free-shipping benefits, broader product selection and faster deliveries are encouraging repeat purchases and attracting customers. The company's expanding logistics infrastructure and investments in automation should enhance fulfillment efficiency, strengthen customer retention and support further marketplace penetration.

Mercado Pago remains a significant growth engine as consumers increasingly rely on the platform for everyday transactions, savings, investments and borrowing. Fintech monthly active users increased 29% year over year, while assets under management grew 67%. MercadoLibre's ability to leverage marketplace transaction data for credit underwriting and customer acquisition provides a competitive advantage. Improving credit card economics as existing customer cohorts mature, alongside stable delinquency trends, reinforces the fintech business's long-term earnings potential.

Advertising and artificial intelligence (AI) are creating additional avenues for monetization and operational efficiency. Advertising revenues increased 58% year over year in U.S. dollar terms, supported by improvements in AI-powered advertising tools and expanding retail media capabilities. The company's partnership with Netflix should extend its connected television advertising reach beginning in early 2027. Meanwhile, stronger engagement across commerce and fintech, expanding affiliate networks and declining per-shipment costs in Brazil provide a foundation for further market share gains and long-term profitability improvements.

Nonetheless, investments in free shipping, fulfillment capacity and affiliate marketing are weighing on near-term profitability. Third-quarter operating income declined 6% year over year, while the operating margin contracted 40 basis points sequentially to 6.3%. Rapid credit portfolio expansion also warrants monitoring amid challenging lending conditions in Brazil and Argentina despite disciplined underwriting practices and healthy asset quality.

The Case for TGT

Target's business transformation is gaining traction as strategic changes across merchandising, pricing and customer experience translate into stronger demand. Third-quarter fiscal 2026 net sales increased 7.1%, while comparable sales rose 5.6%, driven by a 5% jump in comparable traffic. Strong performances across beauty, food and beverage, and Fun 101 highlight encouraging progress in its merchandising strategy. The introduction of Target Beauty Studio, exclusive brand collaborations and an emphasis on affordable, trend-right merchandise should strengthen customer engagement and encourage more frequent shopping trips.

Target is enhancing its omnichannel capabilities through investments in store modernization, supply-chain infrastructure and technology. Comparable digital sales increased 9.8% during the third quarter, reflecting continued momentum across its online platform. Its store-based fulfillment model provides customers with convenient shopping options, including Order Pickup, Drive Up and same-day delivery. Store remodels, network expansion and improved inventory management should enhance product availability and customer convenience. Management's plan to invest $5-$6 billion in capital expenditures in fiscal 2027 is expected to support continued business transformation and growth.

The retailer is broadening its earnings opportunities through expanding non-merchandise businesses. Roundel advertising, Target Circle 360 membership, Target Circle Card profit-sharing revenues and the Target+ marketplace supported nearly 20% growth in non-merchandise sales. These businesses offer attractive monetization opportunities and the potential to strengthen customer loyalty and diversify revenue streams. Meanwhile, AI-powered shopping tools and technology-enabled productivity improvements should enhance the shopping experience, support merchandising decisions and improve operating efficiency.

Target's improving underlying profitability reinforces its recovery prospects. Excluding tariff refund benefits, third-quarter adjusted EPS increased 21%, while gross margin expanded approximately 120 basis points year over year. Management raised its fiscal 2026 net sales growth outlook to around 6% and updated adjusted EPS guidance to $10.65-$11.40, including $2.14 in tariff refund benefits. Although home and apparel remain areas of improvement, targeted assortment changes and pricing initiatives offer opportunities to rebuild momentum.

Earnings Estimate Trends for MELI & TGT

The Zacks Consensus Estimate for MELI's current and next fiscal year earnings per share (EPS) have moved downward over the past 30 days to $36.74 and $51.25, respectively. The consensus mark for MercadoLibre's current fiscal-year sales indicates year-over-year growth of 44.6%, while EPS is projected to decline 6.8%. For the next fiscal year, consensus estimates suggest sales and earnings growth of 29.2% and 39.5%, respectively.

Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

For TGT, the consensus estimates for the current and next fiscal year EPS have moved upward over the past 30 days to $10.94 and $9.68, respectively. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for Target's current fiscal-year sales and EPS indicates year-over-year growth of 5.7% and 44.5%, respectively. For the next fiscal year, estimates suggest a 3.3% increase in sales and an 11.5% decline in earnings.

Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

MELI & TGT's Stock Price Performance

MercadoLibre shares have declined 29.1 over the past year despite sustained growth across its commerce and fintech businesses. Ongoing investments and near-term profitability pressures remain important considerations for investors.

Target shares have surged 98.9% over the same period, alongside encouraging progress in its business transformation, strengthening customer traffic and improving operating performance.

Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

MELI vs. TGT: A Look at Valuation

From a valuation standpoint, MercadoLibre is trading at a forward 12-month price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple of 28.63, below its one-year median of 33.72. The discount offers a relatively attractive valuation given the company's strong growth fundamentals and expanding digital ecosystem, although near-term profitability pressures warrant some caution.

Target currently trades at a forward 12-month P/E multiple of 16.96, above its one-year median of 15.28. The valuation premium could reflect growing investor confidence in the company's improving retail fundamentals, strengthening customer traffic and progress across strategic growth initiatives.

Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

Which Stock Is a Better Bet Now?

MercadoLibre offers compelling long-term growth potential through its expanding commerce, fintech and advertising ecosystem. However, near-term margin pressures, growing credit exposure and downward earnings estimate revisions warrant caution. Target's strengthening customer traffic, differentiated merchandising, expanding digital capabilities and growing non-merchandise businesses reinforce its recovery prospects. Improving underlying profitability, a raised sales outlook, favorable earnings estimate revisions and encouraging share price momentum further strengthen its investment case. These factors position Target as the more compelling investment choice at this juncture.

title: MercadoLibre Grew Revenue 45% as Operating Income Fell 6%. Is It “a Gift at These Prices”?
detail:
MercadoLibre Grew Revenue 45% as Operating Income Fell 6%. Is It “a Gift at These Prices”?
Wiltone Asuncion
Tue, November 24, 2026 at 7:57 AM EST 5 min read
MELI
NU
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
MercadoLibre Grew Revenue 45% as Operating Income Fell 6%. Is It "a Gift at These Prices"? ©@small smiles from Getty Images via Canva, @anyaberkut from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

MercadoLibre's third-quarter revenue rose 45% to $10.75 billion, while operating income fell 6% to $676 million.

Much of the squeeze looks like MercadoLibre's own choice, since rival Sea grew Shopee's profit despite its push into Brazil.

The risk that could last is credit: loans more than 90 days late are rising, and lenders like Nu Holdings trade at a fraction of MercadoLibre's multiple.

At 31x forward earnings, MercadoLibre trades near the low end of its five-year range, and the fourth-quarter report will test analysts' 44% EPS rebound for 2027.

MercadoLibre (MELI:NASDAQ) grew revenue 45% last quarter, yet its stock closed at $1,425.08 on Nov. 23, still about 7% below its Nov. 5 close of $1,530.28, the session after the report.

On Nov. 19, one investor made the case for buying the drop in a post shared on both r/stocks and r/ValueInvesting, titled: "$MELI is a gift at these prices."

The market disagrees, and two other stocks help explain why. Shopee, owned by Sea Limited (SE:NYSE), is the rival whose push into Brazil is a big reason MercadoLibre is spending so heavily on shipping. And Nu Holdings (NU:NYSE) lends to many of the same Brazilian and Mexican consumers that Mercado Pago's credit book is growing into.

The numbers check out

The 45% and the 6% come straight from MercadoLibre's third-quarter release on Nov. 4, which put revenue growth at 41% FX-neutral. MercadoLibre blamed the drop in operating income on more free shipping, new fulfillment capacity added ahead of the holiday peak, and more affiliate marketing spend in Brazil.

Analysts' estimates show normalized EPS dipping this year before a big rebound:

MercadoLibre (MELI): normalized EPS, actual and consensus estimates, $ per share, fiscal 2023-2028 (TIKR)

Consensus has 2026 EPS at $36.66, below 2025's $39.40, then $52.96 in 2027, a 44% jump. Analysts keep trimming that rebound, though: the 2027 estimate is about 6% lower than a month ago.

TIKR tracks 25 analysts on MercadoLibre. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on MercadoLibre, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See MercadoLibre's Analyst Ratings

The margin squeeze is mostly a choice

MercadoLibre's operating margin has more than halved in under two years, from 13.5% in the fourth quarter of 2024 to 6.3% last quarter:

MercadoLibre (MELI): operating (EBIT) margin (%), last 8 quarters (to September 30, 2026) (TIKR)

The shipping spending is starting to pay off. In Brazil, cost per shipment fell 5% from a year earlier in local currency and sat 14% below its level in the first quarter of 2025.

Sea's results suggest the squeeze is mostly MercadoLibre's own doing. Sea CEO Forrest Li said Brazil remained Shopee's fastest-growing market in the third quarter, yet Shopee's adjusted EBITDA rose 45% to $269.2 million on 41% revenue growth. (Shopee's figures cover all its markets, most of them in Southeast Asia.)

Credit is the risk that could last

The bigger risk is the loan book. The credit card is now 47% of MercadoLibre's portfolio, up from 44% a year ago. The company calls it its largest fintech investment, at almost $450 million over the past 12 months, because newer groups of cardholders lose money before they turn profitable.

Loans 15 to 90 days late were 7.0% of the portfolio, close to all-time lows. But loans more than 90 days late rose to 19.3% of the book at Sept. 30, from 18.7% at June 30. Those are the loans closest to being written off, which MercadoLibre does at 360 days.

Nu shows what lending to these consumers can earn: a record $1.1 billion of net income in the third quarter. Yet investors pay just 11x forward earnings for Nu. The more of MercadoLibre's profit that comes from credit, the harder it gets to justify paying nearly 3x Nu's multiple.

Cheap, with one thing left to prove

The poster puts MercadoLibre at about 36x trailing earnings. On TIKR's forward numbers it's cheaper, at 31x, near the bottom of its five-year range:

MercadoLibre (MELI): forward (NTM) P/E, last 5 years (TIKR)

That's half its five-year average of 61x.

At that multiple, MercadoLibre looks cheap for a company growing revenue 45%, and the shipping math is starting to work. The loan book is what keeps it from being a gift. The fourth-quarter report in early 2027 is the next test: an operating margin back near 10%, with loans more than 90 days late holding at or below 19.3%, would go a long way toward proving the poster right.

title: Emerging Markets at Crisis-Era Valuations—Are These 5 Investments Worth the Risk?
detail:
Emerging Markets at Crisis-Era Valuations—Are These 5 Investments Worth the Risk?
Illustration of bull and bear statues beside a digital globe with stock charts and a declining red price graph.
Ryan Hasson, MarketBeat
Mon, November 23, 2026 at 10:30 AM EST 8 min read
MELI
EEM
VWO
NU
MELI NASDAQ
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Key Points

Interested in MercadoLibre, Inc.? Here are five stocks we like better.

The MSCI Emerging Markets Index has entered bear-market territory as semiconductor stocks, a stronger dollar, and political uncertainty weigh on valuations.

The iShares MSCI Emerging Markets ETF offers direct exposure to the index, while the Vanguard FTSE Emerging Markets ETF provides broader diversification at a lower cost.

MercadoLibre, Nu Holdings, and dLocal have fallen sharply despite reporting strong revenue growth or record profits.

The global sell-off in AI and technology stocks has left its mark on the developing world. On Friday, Nov. 20, the MSCI Emerging Markets Index fell for a seventh consecutive session and officially entered bear market territory, now more than 20% below its June peak. It was also the index's worst week since March 2020.

That decline has pushed emerging-market valuations to levels that are difficult to overlook. As of the close on Friday, Nov. 20, the index traded at a forward price-to-earnings ratio (P/E) last seen during the crisis of 2008, well below every other major region. Market participants now have to weigh whether this marks a generational buying opportunity, or whether emerging markets are cheap for good reason, such as forward earnings no longer being as visible or likely as they previously were.

→ Zscaler Got a Boost From Palo Alto, But Now It Has to Deliver

What Triggered the Selling

The pressure has come from several directions at once, and each has compounded the others.

The unwinding of the AI trade has been the biggest single driver. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE: TSM), Samsung Electronics (OTCMKTS: SSNLF), and SK hynix (NASDAQ: SKHY) together make up close to 28% of the MSCI Emerging Markets Index, so a sell-off in chip stocks hits emerging markets harder than almost anywhere else. Taiwan's stock market fell 17.5% in the week to Nov. 20, its worst five-day stretch since 1990.

→ Keysight Technologies: The Tollbooth on the Technology Superhighway

A surging U.S. dollar has added to the strain. The U.S. Dollar Index reached 103.97 on Nov. 19, its highest level since April 2025, before closing at 103.81 on Nov. 20. A stronger dollar tends to weigh on emerging markets by pulling capital back toward the U.S., raising the cost of dollar-denominated debt and eroding the value of local-currency returns for U.S.-based investors.

Interest rate expectations are closely tied to that move. Hotter-than-expected inflation readings have pushed markets to price in a high probability of another Federal Reserve rate hike in December 2026. That has kept U.S. yields elevated and made the higher-risk returns of emerging markets less attractive by comparison.

→ Growing Pains Versus Growth: Is BJ's Wholesale Club a Buying Opportunity?

Geopolitics and oil have also played a role. Energy prices tied to the conflict in the Middle East have fed into U.S. core inflation, while renewed uncertainty around U.S.-Iran relations has boosted safe-haven demand for the dollar.

Finally, Brazil has faced its own shock. Following President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's re-election in the Oct. 25 runoff, the Brazilian real fell more than 11% against the dollar in early trading. On Oct. 26, the Bovespa, Brazil's main stock market index, closed down 13.9%, its largest daily drop since March 2020, as investors weighed concerns over fiscal policy and government spending.

Why Cheap Is Not the Whole Story

The index's low valuation also needs to be viewed in context. Because a handful of chipmakers carry so much weight in the index, its forward multiple partly reflects booming memory and semiconductor earnings estimates. If those estimates prove to be near a cyclical peak, today's discount could narrow from falling earnings rather than rising prices. On the other hand, many emerging-market businesses sit well outside the AI supply chain, including consumer, financial, and payments companies across Latin America. Several are being sold off alongside the chip names despite strong underlying results.

For market participants looking to position for a potential rebound, here are five names worth watching.

iShares MSCI Emerging Markets ETF: The Direct Play on the Index

The iShares MSCI Emerging Markets ETF (NYSEARCA: EEM) tracks the MSCI Emerging Markets Index itself, making it the most direct way to gain exposure to the theme. That also means it carries the index's heavy weighting toward Taiwan, South Korea, and the chip supply chain, which helps explain why it closed Nov. 20 about 25% below its 52-week high.

The fund has slipped almost 2% year to date (YTD) and fallen about 13% over the past month. It is also among the pricier options in the space, with an expense ratio of 0.72%.

For investors who believe the semiconductor sell-off has overshot, however, EEM offers the most direct exposure to a recovery in the very stocks that drove the decline.

Vanguard FTSE Emerging Markets ETF: Broader and Cheaper

The Vanguard FTSE Emerging Markets ETF (NYSEARCA: VWO) offers a meaningfully different mix. It tracks an FTSE index that classifies South Korea as a developed market, so it excludes Samsung and SK hynix entirely, while including Chinese A-shares and a much broader basket of smaller companies.

That difference has shown up in performance. VWO closed Nov. 20 about 18% below its 52-week high, a smaller drawdown than EEM's, and its expense ratio is just 0.06%, a fraction of EEM's. It also yields about 2.3%.

For investors who want broad emerging-market exposure with less concentration in a single industry, VWO may be the more balanced vehicle, although TSMC remains one of its largest holdings.

MercadoLibre: Latin America's E-Commerce and Fintech Leader

MercadoLibre (NASDAQ: MELI) has been caught squarely in the sell-off, closing Nov. 20 at $1,355, down about 33% YTD and roughly 42% below its 52-week high. The stock also recently touched a new 52-week low of $1,333.54.

The selling has had as much to do with margins as with macro. Third-quarter revenue jumped 45% to $10.75 billion, ahead of estimates, but earnings of $8.83 per share missed the $9.27 consensus as operating margin narrowed to 6.3% from 9.8% a year earlier.

Management has been reinvesting heavily, lowering its free shipping threshold and expanding fulfillment capacity, while its fintech arm continues to scale.

Several firms trimmed their targets after the report, but the 20 analysts covering the stock still rate it a Moderate Buy. Their average price target of $2,160.59 implies close to 60% upside potential.

Nu Holdings: Record Profits at a Discounted Price

Nu Holdings (NYSE: NU), the digital bank behind Nubank, has fallen about 33% this year as Brazilian assets sold off following the election. Shares closed Friday at $11.28, about 41% below their 52-week high.

The underlying business, however, continues to post record results. Third-quarter net income reached a record $1.1 billion, up 31% on a currency-neutral basis, with a return on equity of 32%. The company added 3.7 million customers to reach 143 million, and it now serves 65% of Brazil's adult population.

Credit quality remains the key risk to watch, with management noting higher headline delinquency as the loan mix shifts. At nearly 11x forward earnings, though, the stock trades at a modest multiple for its growth, and analysts hold a Moderate Buy consensus with an average target of $18.06.

dLocal: Payments Volume Still Surging

dLocal (NASDAQ: DLO), which helps global merchants accept and send payments across emerging markets, offers exposure that stretches well beyond Latin America. The stock closed Friday at $12.04, down about 15% YTD and roughly 25% below its 52-week high.

Third-quarter total payment volume climbed 77% to $18.3 billion, its eighth straight quarter of growth above 50%, while revenue rose 41% to $398 million and net income hit a record $68 million. The concern is that revenue per dollar processed keeps shrinking, with revenue essentially flat from the second quarter.

The top 10 merchants also accounted for 62% of revenue in the first nine months of the year. Still, the stock trades at about 11x forward earnings, and the seven analysts covering it hold a Moderate Buy consensus with an average target of $18.80, implying almost 56% potential upside.

A Generational Bottom, or Too Early to Tell?

On paper, the valuation case is compelling. Emerging markets are priced at levels last seen around the financial crisis, and several high-quality businesses are being sold alongside the chip stocks that triggered the decline. But the forces behind the sell-off, including a strong dollar, a hawkish Fed, an unwinding AI trade, and political risk in Brazil, have yet to reverse. Until they do, the selling may not be finished. For patient investors, building a watchlist now and waiting for signs that the dollar is peaking and the index is stabilizing may offer a better risk-reward balance than trying to call the exact bottom.

MercadoLibre is home to both a dominant online marketplace (Mercado Libre) and a major fintech business (Mercado Pago), both focused on the Latin American market. It's active in 18 countries and was recently delivering 3.2 billion items annually. It sports 136 million unique buyers and 93 million monthly active users (both numbers as of the third quarter). And it's growing briskly, with net revenue recently up about tenfold since 2020.

So what's going on that would depress the stock? Well, there are some concerns, such as:

Competition has been growing in the fintech realm.

The e-commerce side of the business is potentially facing more competition, too, from outside retail giants.

Geopolitical tensions in Latin America, such as in Brazil, might destabilize the business -- as the more business-friendly candidate didn't win the presidential election.

Profit margins have been shrinking.

Those are legitimate concerns, but they aren't deal-breakers. As MercadoLibre notes, it has built a powerful ecosystem, combining "the region's largest e-commerce platform, its fastest and most reliable logistics network, one of its biggest digital banks, its largest fintech payments processor, and a top-3 digital ads platform -- with a loyalty scheme that ties it all together." That's not easy to compete against.

Meanwhile, the shrinking profit margins are partly due to the company extending more free shipping and credit to shoppers and investing in future growth, such as by expanding its fulfillment capabilities. If I weren't already a shareholder, I'd consider MercadoLibre for my portfolio.
